judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis), so direction rests on statement substance rather than rank. The second (B4.4.1.1.3, under Content Standard B4.4.1.1 'Demonstrate an understanding of many-to-one correspondence in displaying, and reading or interpreting, graphs') has learners compare graphs displaying the same data and explain how they are the same and different — analytic attention to graph features. The first (B4.4.1.2.1, under Content Standard B4.4.1.2 'Construct and interpret pictographs and bar graphs involving many-to-one correspondence') explicitly requires identifying common features of many-to-one graphs and then using that understanding to construct bar graphs or pictographs with title, labelled axes and key/legend for up to 4 categories. Proficiency in comparing/explaining graph similarities and differences plausibly supports success in the construction task, which names feature identification as its entry point; the shift from interpreting existing displays to producing conventioned displays is a substantive extension, not mere repetition. Shared LC tokens ('data', 'graphs') and the weak code-prefix/rank-proximity signals were treated as nomination reasons only. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the full exemplar text was not available.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicator-grain statements about rounding decimals, judged within the same statement type. B4.1.4.1.2 'Round decimals to the nearest tenth' (BASIC 4, rank 0) is extended by B5.1.4.1.3 'Round decimals to the nearest tenth and hundredth' (BASIC 5, rank 1), which retains the tenths skill and adds the hundredths place, a substantive increase in place-value precision. The parent Content Standards corroborate the deepening (B4 develops understanding of decimals in tenths and hundredths with place value; B5 demonstrates understanding of decimal fractions and comparing/adding/subtracting strategies), so proficiency in tenth-rounding supports success with tenth-and-hundredth rounding. Direction is lower-to-higher rank (first_to_second). Both endpoints carry unresolved-ancestry/framework-root fallback and truncated source-evidence warnings, which were not used as positive placement evidence; the judgment rests on the resolved Grade coordinates and the statement texts themselves.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 (rank 0) Indicators sharing the direct parent Content Standard B4.1.1.3 'Demonstrate an understanding of factors, multiples and squared numbers' within Strand 1 Number, Sub-strand 1. B4.1.1.3.3 asks learners to determine the LCM of two numbers up to 100 (multiples), while B4.1.1.3.6 asks learners to represent square numbers using factors (factor structure/representation). These are complementary facets of the same factor/multiple concept cluster and mutually reinforce multiplicative number structure, but neither statement's proficiency is evidenced as supporting success in the other: LCM work does not require square-number representation, and representing squares via factors does not require common-multiple procedures. Same canonical rank with no substantive evidence of developmental direction, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than buildsTowards. Shared parent, code prefix, and the single shared token 'numbers' alone were not treated as sufficient; the pair-specific conceptual coherence in factors/multiples carries the decision. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, so unseen exemplars could alter the picture.
